title: Gene therapy's long road

confidence.note: The 1990 NIH trial, Jesse Gelsinger's death in 1999, the leukemia cases reported in 2003 and the approvals of 2003, 2012, 2015 and 2017 are well documented. Calling DeSilva's treatment the first successful gene therapy is conventional, but very few of the cells in those early trials were actually corrected.

place: National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, Maryland; Philadelphia; Europe
people: Ashanthi DeSilva, patient treated in the 1990 ADA-SCID trial
W. French Anderson and R. Michael Blaese, NIH researchers who led the 1990 trial
Jesse Gelsinger (died 1999), 18-year-old volunteer who died in a gene therapy trial
summary: A corrected gene in a child's immune cells in 1990 promised cures; a death and a run of leukemias showed the risks, and approved treatments in the West took until 2012.
body: In 1990, at the National Institutes of Health, a team led by French Anderson and Michael Blaese gave Ashanthi DeSilva, who had the inherited immune disorder ADA-SCID, infusions of her own T cells carrying a working copy of the missing gene. Optimism collapsed in 1999, when 18-year-old Jesse Gelsinger died in a Pennsylvania trial after a reaction to the delivery virus, and in 2003, when leukemia was reported in five children treated for another form of SCID. China approved Gendicine in 2003; Europe approved Glybera in 2012, the first Western approval; in the United States Imlygic followed in 2015, and Kymriah and Luxturna in 2017.

links.note: Gene therapy depended on the tools for cutting and splicing DNA.
Gene editing offered a way to repair genes rather than add them.
A lawsuit over Gelsinger's death alleged inadequate consent and undisclosed financial conflicts of interest.

title: Evidence-based medicine

confidence.note: The 1991 editorial, the 1992 JAMA article and the 1993 founding of the Cochrane Collaboration are documented in print. The story of how Guyatt chose the name comes from later accounts, and how much the movement has improved care remains argued.

place: McMaster University, Hamilton, Ontario; Oxford, England
people: Archie Cochrane (1909–1988), British epidemiologist and author of *Effectiveness and Efficiency*
David Sackett, McMaster clinical epidemiologist who taught critical appraisal
Gordon Guyatt, McMaster physician who coined the term
summary: A Canadian residency program gave a name to an old demand, that treatments be judged by fair trials rather than habit, and the name spread through medicine within a few years.
body: In 1972 the British epidemiologist Archie Cochrane published *Effectiveness and Efficiency*, a book stressing the importance of randomized trials in identifying which health services do more good than harm. At McMaster University in Canada, David Sackett and colleagues taught doctors to appraise research critically. In 1990 Gordon Guyatt, McMaster's residency coordinator, called his bedside teaching method "scientific medicine"; colleagues bristled at the suggestion that their own practice was unscientific, so he renamed it. "Evidence-based medicine" appeared in a 1991 editorial, and in 1992 an international working group announced it in *JAMA* as a new paradigm. In 1993 the Cochrane Collaboration was founded to review trials systematically, building on an Oxford database of trials in pregnancy and childbirth.

The approach spread into guidelines, journals and medical teaching. Critics have argued that it turns clinical judgment into an algorithmic exercise that is not individualized to the patient. In 2014 Trisha Greenhalgh and colleagues warned of a movement in crisis: the evidence-based label taken over by drug and device makers, more guidelines than anyone could use, and guidelines that map poorly onto patients with several diseases at once.

links.note: The randomized controlled trial is the method the movement ranks highest.
An early comparison of treatments, often claimed as a forerunner.

title: OxyContin and the opioid epidemic

confidence.note: OxyContin's approval and 1996 launch, the 2007 guilty pleas and the CDC's three-wave pattern are documented. How much of the epidemic marketing caused, rather than wider changes in pain treatment, is the subject of continuing litigation and research.

summary: A slow-release painkiller sold on the claim that addiction was rare helped set off an American overdose epidemic that came in three waves.
body: Purdue Pharma launched OxyContin, a slow-release oxycodone taken every 12 hours, in 1996; sales reached $1.1 billion by 2001. Its promotion leaned on the claim that addiction in pain patients was rare, drawing on a five-sentence 1980 letter by Porter and Jick reporting 4 cases of addiction among 11,882 patients, cited hundreds of times, usually without noting that those patients were in hospital. US overdose deaths came in three waves: prescription opioids from 1999, heroin from 2010 and illicit fentanyl from 2013. The Purdue Frederick Company, a Purdue holding, pleaded guilty to misbranding OxyContin in 2007.

myth.tradition: Studies in the 1980s showed that fewer than 1% of patients given opioids for pain become addicted.
myth.record: The claim rested on a brief 1980 letter about patients treated in hospital and a survey of burn units, not on any study of long-term use outside hospital, and most later citations of the letter left out the hospital setting.

links.note: The opioid painkillers descend from morphine.
An earlier era of drugs sold with misleading claims.

title: Dolly the sheep

confidence.note: Dolly's birth on 5 July 1996 and the method are recorded by the Roslin Institute and in the February 1997 paper in *Nature*. Whether cloning shortened her life was long debated; later studies of her clones suggest it did not.

people: Ian Wilmut (1944–2023), embryologist who led the team
Keith Campbell (died 2012), Roslin scientist and key member of the team
summary: A sheep made from a single udder cell proved that an adult, specialized cell still holds the instructions for a whole animal.
body: On 5 July 1996 a white-faced lamb was born to a black-faced Scottish Blackface ewe at the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh. Dolly had been made by fusing a cell from the mammary gland of a six-year-old Finn Dorset ewe with an egg cell, and she was named after Dolly Parton. Sheep had been cloned from embryo cells before; Dolly was the first mammal cloned from an adult cell. Announced to the world in February 1997, she set off worldwide argument about human cloning, and the proof that adult cells could be reset fed later stem cell research.

myth.tradition: Dolly aged prematurely and died young because she was a clone.
myth.record: She was put down at six after a lung cancer caused by a retrovirus that had infected other Roslin sheep, though she had also been treated for arthritis, which fed suspicion about cloning. Four ewes cloned from the same cell line were healthy at about eight.

links.note: Showing that adult cells could be reprogrammed encouraged work on induced stem cells.

title: The MMR scare

confidence.note: The 1998 paper, the 2004 partial retraction, the 2010 full retraction and the findings against Wakefield are matters of record, and very large studies have found no link between MMR and autism.

people: Andrew Wakefield, British gastroenterologist and lead author of the 1998 paper
Brian Deer, journalist whose investigation exposed the fraud
summary: A 12-child case series in *The Lancet* linked the MMR vaccine to autism; it was retracted and shown to be fraudulent, but vaccination rates fell and measles returned.
body: In 1998 the gastroenterologist Andrew Wakefield and 12 coauthors published a case series of 12 children in *The Lancet*, suggesting that the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine might predispose children to bowel inflammation and developmental regression. The study was tiny and uncontrolled, but it drew wide publicity, MMR vaccination rates in Britain fell, and parents demanded single vaccines. Epidemiological studies followed almost immediately and found no link; a 2021 Cochrane review drawing on studies of nearly 1.2 million children found that MMR does not cause autism.

In 2004 ten of the coauthors withdrew the paper's interpretation, and the journal acknowledged that Wakefield had been funded by lawyers acting for parents suing vaccine makers. In 2010 *The Lancet* retracted the paper entirely after Britain's General Medical Council found that the children had been carefully chosen, though the paper called the sampling consecutive, and that invasive tests had been done without proper ethical clearance; Wakefield was struck off the medical register. By 2011 the *BMJ* had published the journalist Brian Deer's evidence of deliberate fraud. Measles came back as coverage fell, with outbreaks in Britain in 2008 and 2009 and more than 300 confirmed cases in Liverpool in 2012.

myth.record: The claim began with a 12-child study later found to be fraudulent, and large studies covering more than a million children have found no link.

links.note: The measles vaccine whose uptake the scare undermined.
Opposition to vaccination is as old as vaccination itself.

title: Stem cells, embryonic and induced

confidence.note: The 1998 and 2006–07 papers, the Hwang fraud and the 2012 Nobel Prize are fully documented. What remains open is how many treatments will reach routine use; most are still in clinical trials.

place: Madison, Wisconsin; Kyoto, Japan; Seoul, South Korea
people: James A. Thomson, Wisconsin biologist who derived human embryonic stem cells
Shinya Yamanaka, Kyoto researcher who created induced pluripotent stem cells
John B. Gurdon, biologist who reprogrammed frog cells in 1962
Woo Suk Hwang, Seoul researcher whose cloned-embryo stem cell claims were fraudulent
summary: Human embryonic stem cells arrived in 1998 amid ethical alarm; in 2006 a Kyoto lab learned to turn ordinary adult cells back into their equivalent.
body: In 1998 a team led by James Thomson in Wisconsin reported the first lines of human embryonic stem cells. From 36 embryos donated by IVF patients they established five lines of pluripotent cells, able in principle to become any tissue of the body. Using embryos raised ethical concerns. In 2005 the field suffered a major scandal, when Woo Suk Hwang of Seoul National University, who had claimed in two *Science* papers to have made patient-specific stem cells from cloned human embryos, was found to have fabricated images and obtained human eggs unethically.

In 2006 Shinya Yamanaka's laboratory in Kyoto showed that four genes could reprogram adult mouse cells into a pluripotent state, and within a year the method worked on human cells. These induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells needed no embryos, and they won Yamanaka the 2012 Nobel Prize, shared with John Gurdon, who had shown in 1962 that the nucleus of a frog's intestinal cell could direct a normal tadpole. Clinical use has come slowly: the first study using iPS-derived cells began in 2014, and by 2019 about 30 trials were testing embryonic stem cell products for conditions such as macular degeneration and spinal cord injury.

links.note: Dolly showed that an adult cell's nucleus could be reset to make a whole animal.
The first human embryonic stem cells came from embryos left over from IVF.
Gene editing is now combined with stem cells to model and treat disease.
